metadata.note: The Erie Railroad's Rochester Branch, Rochester to Avon, 19 miles. Built as the independent Rochester and Genesee Valley Railroad, which completed the six-foot-gauge line from Exchange Street in Rochester to Avon in 1853 and was worked by the Buffalo, Corning and New York; leased to the Buffalo, New York and Erie in 1858; under direct Erie operation from the Erie's 450-year lease of the BNY&E in 1863. At Avon the branch met three other Erie lines -- the Rochester Division main to Painted Post/Corning, the Mount Morris Branch and the Attica Branch -- and Avon was the division point and shop town from 1885. Four miles north of Avon the line crossed the Canandaigua and Niagara Falls Railroad (later the New York Central 'Peanut Line') at grade; that junction, originally Genesee Valley Junction, is the hamlet of Golah, and the diamond there is why a January 1918 federal proposal would have rerouted Erie Attica-branch traffic over the Peanut from Batavia to Golah. The Erie electrified the whole Rochester–Avon–Mount Morris route in 1906-07 and ran an hourly electric commuter service until de-electrification began in 1934. Passenger service ended September 30 1941; the four Erie lines at Avon quit passengers on different dates (Attica Branch April 30 1933, Mount Morris Branch January 20 1940, Rochester Branch September 30 1941, Rochester Division September 28 1947). SPLIT PER RULE 4: three features share this geometry, one per operating company -- Rochester and Genesee Valley 1853-1858, Buffalo, New York and Erie 1858-1863, Erie 1863-1941.
geometry_sources: OpenStreetMap via Overpass API (maps.mail.ru mirror), bbox 42.86,-77.82,43.18,-77.55, all railway=* ways. Graph built from ways tagged old_railway_operator=Erie or operator=Livonia, Avon & Lakeville Railroad, with nodes merged at 25 m, corridor-weighted Dijkstra between the Court Street depot site and the Avon depot site. Result: 30.68 km / 19.06 mi, 181 points, no reversals, 2.65 km of it straight-line bridging (see geometry_quality).
Nominatim geocoding for Golah (42.9703, -77.7161) and Avon (42.9120, -77.7455).
metadata.not_yet_sourced: 1853 vs 1854 for the first passenger train Rochester–Avon (Avon village history says 1853; the Democrat and Chronicle's 'eighty-seven years' in 1941 implies 1854). 1878 vs 1880 for the New York, Lake Erie and Western reorganisation. May 12 vs June 18 1907 for the start of electric operation. Whether the Erie's own approach into Rochester north of Elmwood Avenue followed the surviving east-bank Genesee corridor now tagged PRR/LV in OSM, or its own separate alignment -- the last 1.58 mi is drawn as a straight line for that reason. No period valuation map was consulted, so a relocation of the alignment between 1853 and 1941 cannot be ruled out. All headway_min values except the 1907-1934 hourly electric service are estimates.

properties.line: Rochester and Genesee Valley: Rochester – Avon
properties.geometry_quality: Real-traced from OpenStreetMap for 17.5 of the 19.1 drawn miles: 13.5 mi of surviving track operated by the Livonia, Avon & Lakeville Railroad and tagged old_railway_operator=Erie, plus 1.3 mi of railway=abandoned tagged old_railway_operator=Erie north of Rush, plus 0.5 mi of untagged LA&L track and 0.1 mi of LA&L track tagged old_railway_operator=LV where the branch shares the ex-Lehigh Valley alignment near West Henrietta. APPROXIMATED, 2 legs: (a) a 1.58 mi straight line across Rochester from the last Erie-tagged abandoned right of way at Elmwood Avenue (43.1321, -77.6237) to the Erie's Court Street depot site (43.1530, -77.6102) -- the approach through the city is built over and carries no Erie tagging in OSM, and the corridor that does survive there (OSM ways tagged old_railway_operator=PRR and =LV along the east bank of the Genesee) was not used because it is not confirmed to be the Erie's own track rather than a neighbour's; (b) a 0.08 mi straight bridge across an untraced break at the Genesee Valley Park crossing (43.0936, -77.6492 to 43.0930, -77.6505). Traced+approximated total 19.06 mi against a documented 19 miles Exchange Street (Rochester) to Avon, and against the 34-mile Rochester-Mount Morris electrification figure less the 15-mile Avon-Mount Morris segment (= 19 mi). The drawn line is today's surviving alignment; no evidence was found of a relocation between 1853 and 1941, but this has not been checked against a period valuation map.

segments.note: The Rochester and Genesee Valley Railroad completed its 19-mile six-foot-gauge line from Exchange Street in Rochester south to Avon in 1853, giving Rochester a connection into the New York and Erie system; the Avon village history dates the first passenger train to 1853, while the Democrat and Chronicle's 1941 farewell called it 'eighty-seven years of Erie Railroad passenger service for Rochester', which back-dates to 1854 -- the conflict is unresolved and 1853 is drawn here. Four miles north of Avon the line crossed the Canandaigua and Niagara Falls Railroad at grade; that junction south of Rush was later named Golah. The R&GV was operated in this period by the Buffalo, Corning and New York Railroad, not by its own management. Headway and avg_speed_kmh are estimates, not taken from a timetable.
sources: Segment-level: opening year, mileage, gauge, the Golah crossing and the Buffalo, Corning and New York operating arrangement are named in the RGVRRM Rochester Division history and the Avon village railroad brochure; headway and speed are unsourced estimates.
segments.speed_source: Estimated. No timetable consulted for the 1850s.

segments.note: The Buffalo, New York and Erie Railroad leased the Rochester and Genesee Valley in 1858 and ran it as its Rochester line, feeding Erie trains at Avon. Drawn in the BNY&E's own colour rather than the Erie's because the BNY&E was still an independent lessee in these years; the Erie took the BNY&E itself on a 450-year lease in 1863. Headway and avg_speed_kmh are estimates, not taken from a timetable.

segments.note: The Erie Railway leased the Buffalo, New York and Erie for 450 years in 1863, bringing the Rochester–Avon line under direct Erie operation. Through the Civil War years the number of passenger trains doubled and eventually included sleeping cars working through to New York. Headway and avg_speed_kmh are estimates, not taken from a timetable.
sources: Segment-level: the 1863 lease and the post-Civil-War doubling of passenger trains (including sleepers) are stated in the RGVRRM Rochester Division history; headway and speed are unsourced estimates.

segments.note: New York, Lake Erie and Western Railroad era. The 1880s were probably the high-water mark of passenger service between Rochester and Corning; by 1887 the Erie's new Court Street depot in Rochester (opened May 14 1887, George E. Archer architect) handled roughly 60 train movements a day. Avon became the division point and shop town of the formal Rochester Division in 1885, with the Rochester Branch, the Mount Morris Branch, the Attica Branch and the Corning main all converging there. NOTE: the sibling layer avon_geneseo_mount_morris_railroad.geojson also dates the NY,LE&W era from 1880; other sources put the reorganisation at 1878. Headway and avg_speed_kmh are estimates, not taken from a timetable.
sources: Segment-level: the 1885 division reorganisation with Avon as division point, the 1887 depot and its ~60 daily movements, and the 1880s peak are stated in the RGVRRM Rochester Division history and the Erie Railroad Depot article; headway and speed are unsourced estimates.

segments.note: Erie Railroad era (the NY,LE&W was reorganised under that name in 1895), worked by steam. By the First World War the Corning and Attica branches were down to two passenger trains each way; a January 1918 federal proposal would have shut the Erie's Attica branch between Batavia and Avon and diverted the traffic onto the New York Central 'Peanut' branch from Batavia to Golah, where the Peanut crossed this line. Headway and avg_speed_kmh are estimates, not taken from a timetable.
sources: Segment-level: the wartime two-trains-each-way figure and the 1918 Batavia–Golah diversion proposal are stated in the RGVRRM Rochester Division history; headway and speed are unsourced estimates.

segments.note: Electric era. The Erie electrified the whole route from its Court Street terminus in Rochester through Avon to Mount Morris in late 1906 - March 1907, and ran it as an hourly electric commuter service from about 6am to 11:30pm, Rochester to Mount Morris in roughly 1h10m over 34 miles. The Court Street depot was one of the very few electrified Erie stations. Headway here is the sourced hourly service; the speed figure is derived from the 34 miles / 1h10m timing.
sources: Segment-level: hourly 6am-11:30pm electric service, the 1906-07 electrification of Rochester–Mount Morris and the ~1h10m running time are cited in the sibling layer avon_geneseo_mount_morris_railroad.geojson and in the Erie Railroad Depot and Avon station articles (which give June 18 1907 for the start of electric operation, against May 12 1907 elsewhere -- conflict unresolved).
segments.speed_source: Derived from the sourced 34 miles in about 1h10m Rochester–Mount Morris, including stops.

segments.note: De-electrification began in 1934 and the branch finished out on gas-electric motor cars. The Erie got Public Service Commission approval to drop the service for poor financial return, with buses authorised as a substitute: the last passenger train left Court Street station at 6:15pm on September 30 1941, ending Erie passenger service in Rochester, and the depot was demolished in 1942. Freight continued over the route long afterwards and most of it is still worked today by the Livonia, Avon & Lakeville Railroad -- that is context, not passenger service, and is not drawn. Headway and avg_speed_kmh are estimates, not taken from a timetable.
sources: Segment-level: the September 30 1941 end of service, the 6:15pm final departure from Court Street, the PSC approval and bus substitution, and the 1942 demolition are stated in the RGVRRM article on the end of Erie service in Rochester, the Erie Railroad Depot article and the Avon station article; headway and speed are unsourced estimates.
